extracted.intended_audience: readers, students, and scholars interested in philosophy and literary criticism of humour
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting conceptual dimensions and evaluative lenses for analysing humour as presented in a short philosophical/critical book. Focuses on thematic, ethical, psychoanalytic, historical, and formal aspects of humour discussed by the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does humour make us human?
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigates whether humour is a specifically human capacity ("Does humour make us human?") and how laughter relates to human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider comparative questions (do animals laugh?), philosophical arguments about what distinguishes human laughter, and implications for theories of mind and culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughing at animals / outlandish animals
rubrics_metrics.description: Examines our tendency to laugh at animals and 'outlandish animals' as a theme in humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse why animals figure as comic subjects, examples of animal comedy, and what this reveals about human projection, anthropomorphism, and boundaries between human and non-human.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughing at your body / bodily humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on bodily functions and the body as a target of laughter (chapter: 'Laughing at Your Body').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include physical/fart/embarrassment humour, the role of the body in producing the ridiculous, and how corporeal comedy interacts with taste, disgust, and social norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: The laughing machine / mechanisation and the comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Considers why it's funny when people act like machines or when human action appears mechanised (chapter: 'The Laughing Machine — a Note on Bergson and Wyndham Lewis').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage with Bergsonian ideas about mechanical behaviour and humour; evaluate examples where rigidity, predictability, or dehumanisation produce comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethnic/foreigner humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Explores humour about foreigners and the 'ethicity and ethnicity of humour' (chapter: 'Foreigners are Funny').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how jokes about nationality, ethnicity, and 'the foreigner' function, including stereotyping, xenophobia, social boundary maintenance, and the political/ethical effects of such humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour as sensus communis (shared sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses humour as a form of common sense or communal judgement (chapter: 'The Jokes on All of Us — Humour as Sensus Communis').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider humour's social bonding functions, how jokes rely on shared assumptions, and when humour targets collective vulnerabilities or norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychoanalytic dimension (superego and laughter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigates psychoanalytic accounts of humour, especially the role of the superego and Freud's theories (chapter: 'Why the SuperEgo is Your Amigo — My Sense of Humour and Freud's').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Freudian concepts (repression, release, superego) to evaluate how jokes manage taboo, guilt, and transgression; compare with other psychological accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Darker/ethical side of humour (sexism, racism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledges and critiques the harmful dimensions of humour — how comedy can be 'rife in sexism and racism'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate when humour reinforces oppression or marginalisation; weigh comedic value against ethical consequences; consider arguments that humour can also 'remind us of people we would rather not be.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical and historical frameworks
rubrics_metrics.description: Engages with historical and theoretical sources on humour (references to Bergson, Kant, Bakhtin, Beckett, Wittgenstein, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply philosophical theories (incongruity, superiority, relief), literary-historical contexts, and thinkers cited in assessing or constructing accounts of humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and structure of jokes / comic devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Attends to the formal properties of jokes and comic writing (joke structure, incongruity, satire, l'humour noir, ridicule).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse devices such as incongruity, satire, the ridiculous, timing, and narrative structure when evaluating comedic effect and meaning.
